Here, we asked whether slow waves in DoC can provide insights into the severity of cortical dysfunction or, conversely, into the preservation of residual awareness and recovery potential, by characterizing their spatial, temporal and morphological properties. We analyzed 256-channel EEG recorded during the Local-Global auditory paradigm in 236 DoC patients, including 123 in Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS), 62 in a Minimally Conscious State minus (MCS-) and 29 in MCS plus (MCS+). High-amplitude slow waves were detected as local events, and their density, amplitude and slopes were quantified scalp-wide and channel-wise, by mean level and temporal variability across the recording. Slow-wave features were related to concurrent (Coma Recovery Scale-Revised - CRS-R, Local-Global paradigm) and follow-up (one-year Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended - GOS-E) assessments of consciousness and functional recovery. Associations with MRI-derived measures of cortical integrity and structural connectivity, and differences between anoxic and traumatic etiologies, were also examined. Slow waves were more frequent in less severe DoC patients (i.e., MCS) compared to UWS. Slow-wave slopes were also steeper frontally and increased at a faster rate in patients exhibiting higher levels of consciousness and/or markers of conscious access during the Local-Global paradigm. More frequent and steeper slow waves at baseline further predicted recovery of consciousness and of functional independence at one year. At the individual level, slow-wave features classified states of consciousness above chance (AUC = 0.62 and 0.71 for MCS- and MCS+ versus UWS), whereas outcome prediction remained modest (0.56-0.58). These clinical associations had a structural basis: slow-wave occurrence was greater after traumatic than anoxic injury and scaled with the integrity of subcortico-cortical projection fibers and consciousness-related cortical networks. Contrary to the classical view of delta activity as a non-specific marker of impaired consciousness, prominent spontaneous slow waves indexed behavioral and neurophysiological signs of awareness and better recovery. Beyond reflecting a propensity for pathological bistability, they may also signal the integrity of the networks required to generate them, together with their residual capacity for dynamic regulation.

title: The Effective Visual Acuity of Butterflies in Flight
abstract: The spatial visual acuity of an eye is determined by both the spatial sampling density of the retina and the angular sensitivity of individual photoreceptors. In insect compound eyes, these are respectively characterised by the interommatidial angle, {Delta}{varphi}, and photoreceptor acceptance angle, {Delta}{rho}. During movement, however, finite photoreceptor integration times cause retinal image motion to broaden the effective acceptance angle, potentially degrading spatial resolution beyond its anatomical limit. This problem is especially acute in flying insects, which experience large rotational velocities during locomotion and must actively stabilise gaze to limit retinal image motion. Butterflies present a particularly demanding case because their flight is characterised by large, wingbeat-coupled thoracic oscillations. Here, we quantify how gaze stabilisation limits motion blur in freely flying Monarch butterflies Danaus plexippus by combining free-flight kinematic reconstruction of the head and thorax with separate intracellular measurements of photoreceptor acceptance angles and integration times from quiescent butterflies. We found that, without head compensation, thoracic oscillations would broaden the effective photoreceptor acceptance angle from its quiescent value of 2.17{degrees} to 9.38{degrees} during take-off. Compensatory head movements substantially reduced this motion-induced broadening, limiting the effective acceptance angle to 5.28{degrees}. Nevertheless, this 2.4-fold broadening of effective photoreceptor acceptance angle represents a substantial degradation of spatial acuity in flight, highlighting motion blur as an important constraint on the visual ecology of flying butterflies.

title: Intracranial electrophysiology reveals distinct neural representations of nociception and salience in the human brain
abstract: Neuroimaging studies have shown close overlap between neural representations of nociceptive stimuli and non-nociceptive, salient stimuli (such as low-probability sounds), leading to the proposal that nociception and salience share a common neural substrate in the human brain. Here we use high-resolution intracranial recordings from 13 neurosurgical patients (2,018 total electrodes) to show that neural representations of nociception and salience are anatomically and functionally distinct in the human brain. 77% of 107 electrodes that encoded nociceptive stimuli did not encode low-probability sounds ("nociceptive representations"), whereas 23% encoded both nociceptive and low-probability sounds ("salience representations"). Nociceptive representations were distinct from salience representations in terms of anatomical prevalence (posterior insula, inferior parietal, and perirolandic cortex vs. anterior insula, thalamus, and inferior frontal gyrus), timing (nociception preceded salience by 120 ms on a trial-by-trial basis), and function (intracranial electrical stimulation was more likely to cause sensory experience when applied near nociceptive representations, as compared to salience representations). These results provide strong evidence that nociception and salience have distinct neural substrates in the human brain, and that selective measurement of these distinct processes may help understand patient-to-patient variability in chronic pain and develop personalized brain stimulation treatments.

title: Biophysical modeling of excitation/inhibition imbalance in Alzheimer's disease
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves early sensory and perceptual changes that can precede memory decline. We developed a two-layer rate-based neural model of early and higher visual areas with feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connections to examine how excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance shapes visual motion perception in AD. METHODS: Using Motion-Induced Position Shift and Altered Motion Repulsion stimuli, we factorially manipulated excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) subfield power and connectivity to examine their effects on illusion representation across visual layers. RESULTS: Increased E, decreased I, and increased E/I reduced illusion representation, consistent with reduced illusion susceptibility in AD, whereas the converse increased illusion representation, reflecting neurotypical processing. Higher-level layer 2 representations were more resistant to E/I perturbations than lower-level layer 1. Illusion representation was less affected by E/I increases in intra-areal (recurrent) connectivity than in inter-areal (feedforward/feedback) connectivity. DISCUSSION: This mechanistic framework links E/I balance and connectivity to altered visual motion illusion representations in AD and suggests that E/I and connectivity measures may provide probes of early AD neurobiology. The framework may also generalize beyond vision.

title: Hippocampal extracellular matrix remodeling and temporally distinct glial reorganization following peripheral injury
abstract: Chronic pain is frequently accompanied by anxiety and other affective disturbances, but the molecular and cellular changes linking peripheral injury to persistent alterations in brain function remain incompletely defined. The hippocampal extracellular matrix (ECM) regulates synaptic plasticity, cellular signaling, and neuroimmune interactions and may therefore contribute to pain-related central plasticity. We used a tibial fracture/cast immobilization model to examine temporal changes in hippocampal ECM, glial morphology, and affective behavior following peripheral injury. Behavioral testing was performed at 3, 7, and 20 weeks after injury, while high-dimensional morphometric analysis of microglia and astrocytes was performed at 1, 3, 7, and 20 weeks. Hippocampal ECM associated molecular signals were mapped at the chronic stage using decellularization coupled with MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry imaging. Injured mice developed mechanical hypersensitivity and reduced exploration in two anxiety related paradigms during the early and chronic stages, with these behavioral phenotypes no longer detected at 20 weeks. At 7 weeks, injury was associated with changes in hippocampal ECM-associated peptide signals, including reduced signals corresponding to four ECM-associated proteins. Microglia and astrocytes exhibited distinct, time-dependent changes in density and multidimensional morphology, with some alterations persisting after behavioral measures returned toward control levels. In vitro, BV2 microglia exhibited rigidity-dependent changes in morphology, phagocytic behavior, and calcium signaling. Together, these findings define a temporally evolving hippocampal ECM and glial phenotype following peripheral injury and identify matrix biomechanics as a candidate regulator of microglial function.

title: Disease stage-sensitive MFSD2A-caveolae axis insigates hippocampal blood-brain barrier disruption in Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) malfunction contributes to pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms that confer hippocampal endotheliocytes vulnerability remain unclear. Here we identify loss of endothelial major facilitator superfamily domain-containing protein 2A (MFSD2A), a suppressor of caveolae-mediated transcytosis, as an early and hippocampus-specific feature of AD-associated vascular impairment. In post-mortem human AD brains, reduction in hippocampal MFSD2A was accompanied with increased levels of caveolin-1 and perivascular albumin extravasation. Analysis of human single-nucleus transcriptomic data further demonstrated that vascular expression of MFSD2A declined during transition from mild cognitive impairment to established AD. In APP/PS1 mice, MFSD2A loss occurred early in hippocampal microvessels and coincided with disproportionately high hippocampal BBB leakage and reductions in GLUT1 and claudin-5, despite broader amyloid deposition throughout other brain regions. Restoration of endothelial MFSD2A using an AAV-BR1-based vascular vector during early stage of amyloid pathology, reduced albumin extravasation and preserved GLUT1 and claudin-5. Early intervention also reduced amyloid plaque burden and plaque-associated neuritic dystrophy, whereas this treatment during established amyloid pathology, although modifying selected endothelial markers, failed to reverse BBB leakage, amyloid pathology, or cognitive impairment. Sustained MFSD2A restoration from the early disease stage provided the greatest protection, preserving hippocampal BBB integrity, reducing amyloid and neuritic pathology, improving long-term potentiation and ameliorating spatial learning and memory deficits. These findings define endothelial MFSD2A loss as a disease stage-sensitive mechanism of hippocampal BBB vulnerability and highlight the MFSD2A-caveolae axis as a therapeutic target for early-stage AD.

title: Accurate Hippocampal Electric Field Modeling for Electroconvulsive Therapy: Numerical Accuracy and Convergence
abstract: Accurate hippocampal electric field (E-field) prediction is important for individualized electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) dosing and emerging deep-brain stimulation approaches such as temporal interference. Because hippocampal fields are far weaker than those beneath the stimulation electrodes, they are highly sensitive to tissue interfaces, conductivity contrasts, and numerical discretization, so numerical error can rival the physical uncertainties of anatomy and conductivity. We investigate this numerical component of hippocampal dosimetry using individualized head models from eleven ECT patients. Identical head40 segmentations, comprising 40 tissue compartments including the bilateral hippocampi, were simulated with three independent numerical methods: a charge-based boundary-element fast multipole method (BEM-FMM), a voxel-based hexahedral finite-element solver, and a conformal tetrahedral finite-element solver. For each, resolution was increased systematically and convergence assessed from the average hippocampal E-field magnitude. At the highest attainable resolutions, the three methods agreed closely, differing by 6%-7% in the left hippocampus and 9%-12% in the right. At default or coarse resolutions, however, they disagreed by 28.8% on average and up to 50.3% in the right hippocampus. Numerical convergence should therefore be established before differences are attributed to anatomical or conductivity uncertainty, and independent-solver agreement provides a practical basis for reliable hippocampal dosimetry.

title: Longitudinal Impacts of Sex-Steroid Hormones on Cerebellar Structure in Adulthood are Sex Differentiated
abstract: Sex-steroid hormones influence brain structure across aging, but their relationship to the cerebellum, a region implicated in cognition and vulnerable to age-related decline, remains poorly characterized, particularly longitudinally and across both sexes. We examined whether 17{beta}-estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone relate to cerebellar volume across two timepoints, and whether these relationships differ by sex. In a mixed-sex sample of aging adults (Baseline N = 137; Year 1 N = 93), free salivary hormones and cerebellar lobular volumes were quantified. Linear regression tested cross-sectional, predictive, and change-score hormone-volume associations, and formal hormone-by-sex interactions, in a priori primary and secondary cerebellar lobules of interest. Hormone-cerebellum relationships were consistently sex-differentiated. Estradiol change related to Crus I volume change in opposite directions in males and females, a dissociation extending across bilateral Crus I and Lobule VI, and Right Crus II. In females, greater increases in testosterone were associated with greater decline in Left Crus I and Right Lobule V volumes. In males, testosterone showed no significant associations in primary analyses, however, increases in estradiol were associated with larger volumes. Progesterone showed a male-specific cross-sectional association with Crus II. Several relationships ran opposite to the direction predicted by estradiols established neurotrophic role. Sex-steroid influences on the aging cerebellum are sex-differentiated, regionally specific, and may not be predicted exclusively by cortical or female-focused models. These findings establish the cerebellum as a potential site of sex-specific hormonal influence on brain aging and also further highlight the complexity of the impact of sex-steroid hormones on the aging brain.

title: Impaired value estimation over space explains turn-induced freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease: A cortico-basal ganglia-inspired reinforcement learning model
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) gait is characterized by reduced walking speed, short shuffling steps, increased double stance time, and increased step time variability. The most debilitating symptom in PD is freezing of gait (FOG), a context-dependent locomotion arrest, mostly occurring while encountering turns, obstacles, and narrow pathways. FOG is more pronounced during turning, a complex task that challenges motor planning and execution. Here, we simulate this phenomenon using a computational model inspired by the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry, based on reinforcement learning (RL) principles. In the model, the agent was trained to learn a value profile while navigating a path that involved turning. To simulate PD conditions, we clamped the temporal difference (TD) error, typically associated with dopaminergic signaling. Our model results show that compared to healthy controls (HC), PD non-freezers and PD freezers exhibit a reduction in turning velocity and step length, alongside an attenuated compensatory step-width widening at the sharpest turn, more pronounced in PD freezers, who additionally show increased step time variability. These kinematic impairments worsen during tighter turns. Ultimately, this model implicates FOG as a problem of impaired estimation of value over space and could potentially represent a generalized deficit in gait impairments in PD.

title: Phase-targeted Poisson closed-loop peripheral nerve stimulation modulates sensorimotor oscillations in human MEG
abstract: Closed-loop brain stimulation offers a promising approach for modulating neural oscillations, but the mechanisms of phase-dependent neuromodulation remain poorly understood. We developed a real-time MEG-based closed-loop system delivering median nerve stimulation using a phase-modulated Poisson process. Sixteen healthy participants (11 female, 5 male) underwent open-loop characterization followed by closed-loop testing of eight phase-offset conditions (0 degrees-315 degrees), each paired with a statistically matched replay control. Closed-loop stimulation induced robust phase-dependent modulation (14.21 +/- 8.24%) versus replay (7.03 +/- 2.95%; p = 0.0003), with consistent phase specificity across participants (circular mean: 70.2 degrees, referenced to each individual's dominant frequency). At the group level, alpha oscillations (8-12 Hz) showed bidirectional modulation (mean boost: +21.0 +/- 19.9% at 0 degrees-135 degrees; mean suppression: -13.3 +/- 10.8% at 180 degrees-315 degrees), while beta oscillations (13-30 Hz) showed predominantly unidirectional suppression (-9.3 +/- 9.6%). Successful fixed-frequency targeting required alignment with each individual's natural peak. Misalignment led to different phase shifts producing power at different frequencies, a phenomenon we term phase-frequency coupling. Dynamic frequency tracking (8-30 Hz) automatically identified and targeted each individual's natural peak, achieving robust bidirectional modulation without prior knowledge of peak location. These findings demonstrate that real-time phase-locked peripheral nerve stimulation selectively modulates sensorimotor oscillations beyond statistically matched open-loop stimulation. The distinct phase-excitability relationships of alpha and beta oscillations, together with the importance of aligning stimulation with individual natural peaks, establish principled guidelines for personalized closed-loop neuromodulation.

title: Connectomics by Sequencing Reveals Self-Organizing Principles of Neuronal Networks in Cerebral Organoids
abstract:
Functional neural networks emerge as developing neurons form synaptic connections. Revealing how these connections are organized and perturbed in disease requires linking single-neuron connectivity to molecular state across thousands of networks, which is challenging with current methods. We developed COSCO (Connectomics by Sequencing in Cerebral Organoids), combining barcoded monosynaptic rabies tracing with single-cell RNA sequencing to reconstruct over 10,000 networks across organoids. We demonstrate that organoid circuitry self-organizes into stereotyped network motifs governed by cell-intrinsic wiring rules aligning with features of mouse cortical connectivity. Projecting network topology onto transcriptomic space reveals that wiring correlates with cell-adhesion and synaptic gene expression programs. In a Tuberous Sclerosis Complex model, pathological hyperexcitability coincides with topological rewiring: mutant networks become more heterogeneous, driven by the transcriptional distribution of upper layer excitatory cell states. This work establishes cerebral organoids as a model to study self-organization of human connectivity, and its disruption in neurodevelopmental disease.

title: Objective markers of altered neural gain dissociate tinnitus and self-reported listening problems in individuals with exceptional hearing thresholds
abstract: Many individuals experience problems that are undetected by standard hearing tests, such as persistent tinnitus and difficulties understanding speech in background noise. Here, we report evidence of altered neural gain in young adults with self-reported listening problems despite exceptional hearing thresholds. Individuals reporting persistent tinnitus (the daily percept of sound in the absence of an external source) exhibited elevated thresholds of the middle ear muscle reflex, suggestive of altered gain in brainstem reflexive circuits, and reduced cortical responses to auditory spatial cues conveyed in the temporal fine structure of low-frequency sounds. Moreover, in both groups, greater self-reported speech-in-noise difficulties were associated with higher magnitude cortical responses, particularly at the highest stimulus intensity, consistent with elevated neural gain. Using a conceptual model, we demonstrate how damage to high-threshold auditory nerve fibres innervating cochlear nuclei can account for reduced activity of binaural neurons sensitive to the temporal fine structure of low-frequency sounds, generating a compensatory increase in neural gain in higher brain centres that impacts listening in complex environments.

title: cyto7: an open, vertex-level cortical type atlas of the human cortex
abstract: The cerebral cortex is organized along a gradient of laminar complexity, indexed principally by the emergence and granularity of layer IV and by the size of layer III neuron somata, and cortical types are the ordered categories along it. The Structural Model builds on that gradient to predict laminar connectivity, plasticity and disease vulnerability (Barbas and Rempel-Clower, 1997; Garcia-Cabezas et al., 2019). Existing digital cortical-type maps are area-level: they assign one type per classical area and cannot represent a type boundary that runs through an area. We release cyto7, an open, vertex-level, seven-type cortical-type atlas delineated on the fsaverage surface following the Garcia-Cabezas protocol and revised by the protocol's authors. We distribute the atlas with a reusable quality-control and support framework. A topological audit reports the map against four spatial rules that follow from cortical type analysis and the dual origin of the neocortex theory: neighbouring vertices differ by at most one type, the least complex cortex forms one continuous limbic belt, eulaminate II forms a single matrix enclosing a few holes, and eulaminate III and koniocortex form isolated islands. These were imposed during construction rather than tested, and the audit reports what imposing them cost. A vertex-wise benchmark against the existing area-level map, one type per von Economo-Koskinas area, shows exact agreement at 52.5% of vertices, with disagreement almost always a single level and concentrated inside the large, heterogeneous areas that a single areal label cannot resolve. Where the two maps disagree, cyto7's label better matches the independent multimodal profile in 60.1% of pooled feature-by-vertex comparisons, against 46% under a rotation null and 54% under granularity-matched alternative partitions (p = 0.020), the harder of the two. A per-vertex anatomical support score, computed from anatomy alone, states how strongly each hand-drawn label is backed by the anatomical evidence, and is deliberately not a calibrated error probability. We then validate cyto7 against independent brain measures not used to define it, under a spatial-autocorrelation (spin) null with FDR control. Intracortical myelin (T1w/T2w) increases, cortical thickness decreases, and the principal functional-connectivity gradient reverses along the type axis (all q of about 0.006 or less). Source-reconstructed resting-state MEG dynamics also track the axis: the intrinsic timescale shortens toward koniocortex (rho of about -0.46) and survives the null, as do the spectral centroid and the slow/fast band-power ratio, whereas the aperiodic 1/f exponent does not. The laminar marker genes are where cyto7 differs most from a quantisation of a continuous map: it shows a larger absolute correlation with the layer-IV marker RORB (rho = +0.78) and the layer-V marker FEZF2 (-0.59) than seven-level septiles of myelin, of the functional gradient or of a histological gradient, on four of five markers, while tying or losing to those septiles on the macroscale proxies. These are larger observed associations against three tested quantisations, not a test that the differences between maps are reliable, and they do not establish the accuracy of any individual boundary. Defined from anatomy alone, cyto7 recovers the sensorimotor-to-association hierarchy and, on these markers, some of the laminar signal underlying it. It is released with its full pipeline and an uncalibrated anatomical support score as a reusable substrate for structure-function and modelling studies.
author_corresponding_institution: Neuroelectrics Barcelona SLU (Spain); Barcelona Computational Foundation, Barcelona, Spain.

title: A dynamical attractor computes reward prediction in the basal forebrain
abstract: Phasic ensemble bursting in subcortical neuromodulatory systems such as the basal forebrain (BF) provides a powerful format for broadcasting reward-prediction signals. These bursts encode reward prediction by varying population amplitude, yet their internal structure, reflected in cell-to-cell amplitude relationships, remains conserved. How neural circuits reconcile these competing constraints remains unknown. Here we show that BF bursting is generated by a dynamical attractor: burst structure is imposed not by feedforward inputs but by recurrent circuit dynamics, while burst amplitude is determined by approximately linear integration across concurrent inputs. Optogenetic activation of BF neurons expressing natriuretic peptide receptor 3 (Npr3) outside the behavioral task reproduced the low-dimensional dynamics of natural cue-evoked bursting, preserving the temporal envelope and cell-to-cell amplitude relationships across stimulation patterns. Critically, unilateral activation of non-overlapping Npr3 populations in either hemisphere recruited the full bilateral ensemble into the same native trajectory, showing that restricted inputs can nevertheless recruit the full ensemble. Matched ipsilateral and contralateral onset latencies exceeding 25 ms implicated recurrent interactions beyond the BF. Despite the conserved structure, population burst amplitude varied with stimulation strength and summed approximately linearly across concurrent unilateral inputs. This linear summation extended to natural sensory input during behavior: adding Npr3 stimulation to auditory cues increased cue-evoked burst amplitude, improved detection, and reduced subsequent reward responses, consistent with stronger reward prediction producing smaller reward prediction errors. Thus, a low-dimensional dynamical attractor preserves a shared BF burst structure across diverse inputs while integrating concurrent inputs into a scalar burst amplitude that encodes reward prediction.
author_corresponding_institution: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

title: Individualized Gabor Flicker for Well-Tolerated Neural Entrainment During Working Memory
abstract: Rhythmic visual stimulation offers a non-invasive means of modulating oscillatory brain activity, but conventional flicker may induce considerable visual discomfort. We developed an individualized Gabor flicker stimulation designed to balance neural entrainment and tolerability. In Experiment 1, thirty-four participants passively viewed Plain and Gabor flickers presented at their individual alpha frequency (IAF), IAF - 2 Hz, or IAF + 2 Hz, and at threshold-adjusted or full intensity. Steady-state visual evoked potential signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was highest at IAF and increased with intensity. Plain and Gabor flickers produced comparable overall SNR, but Gabor flicker was rated as substantially more comfortable and less mentally fatiguing, with stimulation at IAF providing the most favorable balance between neural entrainment and tolerability. In Experiment 2, the optimized stimulation parameters were applied during a retro-cue working memory task using individualized theta and alpha frequency flickers. Stimulation increased SNR and inter-trial phase coherence relative to a non rhythmic Natural condition. No behavioral benefit was observed in the full sample. However, an exploratory subgroup analysis indicated higher accuracy with theta stimulation of cued representations and alpha stimulation of uncued representations than in the Natural condition among participants who showed limited baseline retro-cue benefits. These findings show that individualized Gabor flicker can provide robust and well-tolerated neural entrainment during passive viewing and working memory retention, although its behavioral effects may vary across individuals according to their cognitive performance.

title: Transient Vascular Cell Integration and Intrinsic Media-Stimulated Endothelial Activation Reveal Diabetic Retinopathy Signatures in Human Retinal Organoids
abstract: Retinal organoids (ROs) model human retinogenesis but remain avascular and lack immune components, limiting their utility for studying vascular retinopathies. We generated vascular organoids (VOrs) from human pluripotent stem cells and evaluated their integration into developing ROs. Dissociated VOr cells (day 12 or day 30) were seeded onto 2D retinal neuroepithelium before 3D transition, followed by long-term culture to day 210. VOr derived cells migrated into ROs and transiently persisted. V30 ROs preserved retinal lamination, major neuronal subtypes and light evoked retinal ganglion cell responses comparable to non vascularised controls, whereas media-only ROs cultured in proangiogenic conditions showed structural disorganisation and reduced neuronal survival. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed an endogenous, inflammatory endothelial-like population with partial endothelial-to-mesenchymal features and a perivascular fibroblast-like cluster in pro-angiogenic media only RO controls. The endothelial-like cell cluster was significantly enriched for genes upregulated in human retinal endothelial cells exposed to high glucose, indicating a diabetic retinopathy like transcriptional state. Microglia like and border associated macrophage populations were present across all conditions, with developmental shifts in morphology and marker expression. Our findings define conditions under which vascular cells can be incorporated into human ROs without disrupting retinal architecture, while uncovering an intrinsic capacity for inflammatory endothelial activation that partially recapitulates diabetic retinopathy. This work advances the engineering of vascularised, immunocompetent retinal models and highlights endogenous vascular immune programmes that must be considered when modelling retinal disease in vitro.

title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

title: Distilling Trial-Level EEG Variability into Participant Representations: Neurophysiologically Constrained Graph Learning in ADHD
abstract: Extracting stable individual-level representations from noisy and variable trial-wise EEG remains a major challenge in computational cognitive neuroscience. We developed a spatiotemporal graph attention network to analyze Go/NoGo EEG from children and adolescents with and without ADHD. The framework combines ERP-informed temporal windows, phase-synchrony graph priors, and trial-to-participant transfer learning, making both information routing and representation geometry explicitly testable. The model learned reproducible attention trajectories, yet ADHD and control participants did not differ reliably in spatial attention allocation. Instead, group-related structure emerged in compact participant-level embeddings that distilled trial-level variability and retained discriminative information beyond convolutional representations. Performance exceeded a convolutional neural network comparison, but the central advance is methodological: neurophysiologically constrained graph learning can reveal where diagnostically relevant information emerges within the analytical pipeline. This provides a framework for developing auditable cognitive-neurophysiological markers of neurodevelopmental variation.
author_corresponding_institution: TU Dresden, Universitatsklinikum Carl Gustav Carus

title: Glia-enriched human brain organoids for studying developmental alterations in leukodystrophies
abstract: Leukodystrophies (LKD) comprise mostly inherited white matter disorders whose developmental origins and underlying pathomechanisms remain poorly understood. Progress has been limited by restricted access to human primary tissue and by the inability of animal models to fully recapitulate human neurodevelopment. Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural organoids provide an alternative approach, but most culture systems do not capture later, glia-rich developmental stages relevant to these diseases. Recent studies have shown that appropriate patterning cues and long in vitro differentiation can generate neuroglial spheroids comprising multiple neuronal and macroglial populations, including mature oligodendrocytes. Here, we adapt the human oligodendrocyte (hOLS) spheroid platform to establish 3D models of globoid cell leukodystrophy (GLD), 4H leukodystrophy (4H), and Canavan disease (CD). Here we adapt this organoid platform to establish 3D models of globoid cell leukodystrophy (GLD), 4H leukodystrophy (4H), and Canavan disease (CD). Across 150 days of differentiation, hOLS from different genetic backgrounds displayed largely comparable growth kinetics and developmental trajectories, comprising multiple neuroglial cell types with predominantly ventral forebrain and midbrain identities. Comparison of LKD and control hOLS revealed both shared and disease-specific alterations, with prominent transcriptional changes in lysosomal, metabolic, and stress-response pathways. Lineage-resolved pathway analysis further identified signatures across individual LKDs, including mitochondrial and translational stress in GLD glial lineages, disruption of RNA metabolic and cell-cycle pathways in 4H, and prominent astrocyte-centered metabolic dysregulation in CD. Our results establish hOLS as a human 3D in vitro platform for studying the impact of LKD-associated genetic variants on early neural development and for dissecting lineage-specific disease vulnerability.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Emma Center for Personalized Medicine, Emma Children's Hospital, Amsterdam UMC

title: Psychedelics restructure information in the human brain
abstract: How do psychedelic drugs alter human brain function? Answering this question relies on our ability to understand how information is stored, transferred, and transformed across the cortex. Here, we leverage a precise mathematical framework for multivariate information decomposition to construct the first comprehensive picture of these processes across five compounds: LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and 5-MeO-DMT (N=80). We provide a formal and empirical explanation of major prior results, revealing sets of competing underlying phenomena masked by extant approaches. We extend this analysis to novel higher-order phenomena, and we demonstrate how all of these observations can emerge from a minimal generative model in which neural populations operate with reduced self-coupling. In sum, our results suggest that the psychedelic brain is one in which cortical populations become alike, but not necessarily together. This has important implications for models of how psychedelics reorganize brain dynamics to alter subjective experience and alleviate mental health conditions.

title: "Spilling-in" versus "Filling-in": Disentangling bottom-up drive from predictive completion in human V1 to V3
abstract: It is well established that responses in visual areas are a combination of bottom-up stimulus driven input and top-down input driven by expectation. However, it has been difficult to quantify the differential strength of these components, and how they vary across the visual hierarchy. Here, we introduce a method for dissociating bottom-up and top-down contributions in early retinotopic areas (V1-V3). Using a log-scaled bar stimulus, we measured BOLD responses under full-field vs. central scotoma conditions. Using the full-field stimulus, we estimated pRFs in human visual cortex 17 (V1-V3).

title: Preconceptional social isolation alters inflammatory and transcriptional signalling across the placenta-fetal brain axis
abstract: Maternal depression and psychosocial adversity during pregnancy are associated with altered offspring neurodevelopment, yet the molecular processes linking maternal state to the developing fetus remain incompletely understood. The placenta is positioned to sense and respond to maternal physiological signals, but how placental molecular responses relate to those in the developing brain is unclear. Here, we used a mouse model of prolonged social isolation initiated before conception and maintained throughout pregnancy to investigate inflammatory and transcriptional alterations across matched placenta and fetal-brain samples at gestational day 18. Maternal social isolation altered cytokine profiles in both tissues and induced extensive transcriptional changes in the placenta, with a more restricted response in the fetal brain. Functional analyses identified alterations in placental immune, metabolic and transport-related programmes and fetal-brain immune, neuronal and proliferative processes. Although sex-stratified analyses revealed different transcriptional profiles in male and female tissues, formal maternal housing x fetal-sex interaction testing did not identify significant gene-level interaction effects. Cross-tissue co-expression analysis initially identified extensive covariation between social-isolation-responsive placental and fetal-brain modules; however, most associations were attenuated after accounting for their shared relationship with maternal housing. An exposure-independent network analysis nevertheless identified an inverse pregnancy-level association between a placental module enriched for immune and interferon-related signalling and a fetal-brain module enriched for cell-cycle and proliferative processes. Together, these findings show that prolonged maternal social adversity is associated with coordinated but tissue-distinct molecular alterations across the placenta-fetal brain axis and demonstrate the importance of distinguishing parallel responses to a common maternal environment from direct cross-tissue molecular coupling.

title: Volitional control of a recurrent brain computer interface via covert reinforcement of endogenous reward networks
abstract: Recurrent brain-computer interfaces (rBCIs) deliver targeted stimulation to one brain region based on neural activity recorded and processed in real-time at another. In a volitionally controlled rBCI, the user must also learn to intentionally produce the triggering neural activity, a process typically facilitated by an external reward. However, reliance on an external reward introduces a delay between the triggering event and reinforcement that can slow association between the two and, ultimately, control of the rBCI (particularly for neural activity not directly related to an observable behavior such as a goal-directed movement). The constraint to an external reward also limits studies of neural dynamics during natural, free behavior. In contrast, delivering activity-dependent stimulation directly to the brain's own reward centers - i.e., covert reinforcement - would bypass the need for external feedback, enabling precise temporal coupling between triggering events and reward and allowing for unrestrained rBCI use. Here, we show that rats can gain volitional control of an rBCI using activity-dependent electrical stimulation of the medial forebrain bundle as a sole reinforcer. Animals successfully learned to modulate motor unit discharge rates as well as specific electrocorticographic frequency bands (beta and gamma) to self-trigger stimulation. Furthermore, rats demonstrated flexible control by independently modulating distinct spectral features from the same cortical site. These findings suggest that covert reinforcement of endogenous reward networks can drive operant conditioning of specific neural signals during unrestrained behavior, opening new avenues for adaptive BCIs and closed-loop psychiatric therapies.
author_corresponding_institution: Washington University in St. Louis School of Medicine

title: Distinct cortical networks associated with subregions of the hippocampal-entorhinal system in the first two years of human life
abstract: Episodic memory critically depends on the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex. Despite a rapid developmental change in human episodic memory during the first two years of life, little is known about the developmental trajectory of the hippocampal-entorhinal circuitry during this critical time period. In the current study, we collected high-quality precision fMRI data from five typically developing infants over the time period between 1 and 2 years of life and examined, in great anatomical detail, the developmental profile of distinct parts of the infant hippocampal-entorhinal system and their coupling with distinct cortical networks. We show that already at around 1 year of age, subdivisions of the canonical default network (DN) are fully dissociated at the neocortex and are differently associated with the hippocampal-entorhinal system, with tentatively differential developmental trajectories. While the DN-A, associated with episodic simulation, coupled with the anterior hippocampus and the medial part of the entorhinal cortex, the DN-B, associated with social cognition, showed significantly weaker connectivity with the hippocampal-entorhinal system. Furthermore, the parietal memory network coupled with the posterior hippocampus and the lateral part of the entorhinal cortex. Exploratory longitudinal results suggest that associations of the DN-B with the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex increase towards the end of the second postnatal year, and the associations of the parietal memory network become more topographically restricted to the posterior hippocampus. These networks and their differential maturation may provide the basis for important developments in episodic memory and social cognition in the second postnatal year and suggest that potentially unique properties of human hippocampal-entorhinal circuitry may emerge latest in development.
author_corresponding_institution: Kavli Institute for Systems Neuroscience (NTNU), University of Oxford

title: Neural circuit mechanisms for multi-tasking
abstract: Neural activity during performance of a cognitive or motor task is often described as lying on a low-dimensional manifold in the space of all possible activity patterns. When multiple tasks are performed, an individual brain region's activity may generate multiple such manifolds. Several models have been introduced to explain this capability, each with different assumptions concerning architecture and inputs. Here, we develop a theory of multi-tasking according to which models and experimental paradigms can be organized. We introduce a distinction between sequential and simultaneous multi-tasking, the performance of one task at a time or multiple in parallel. We show that interference between tasks often prevents multi-tasking and introduce a model of ``task barcodes" that circumvents this problem and parameterizes a neuronal population's task selectivity. Our theory reveals categorical distinctions between neural circuit mechanisms supporting multi-tasking that can be probed using physiological recordings.

title: Huntingtin and Celsr3 Orchestrate Spontaneous Long-Distance Spinal Cord Regeneration
abstract: Spontaneous spinal cord regeneration is an endogenous process operational in diverse vertebrate and select mammalian species. Yet despite resulting in functional regeneration, axonal regrowth dynamics as well as underlying molecular programs are largely unknown. Live-cell imaging following laser axotomy of individual zebrafish spinal cord M-cell axons reveals a time-sensitive multistep process. From a genetic screen we uncover previously unrecognized roles for two evolutionary conserved genes, celsr3 and huntingtin (htt) in spontaneous spinal cord regeneration. Specifically, we find that htt is critical to initiate a transcriptional injury response in regenerating M-cells, enabling their axon to traverse the injury site. Once axons cross the injury site celsr3 functions to increase growth rates, while both celsr3 and htt function to sustain long-range axonal growth. Moreover, we show that htt is dispensable for optic nerve and peripheral motor neuron regeneration, and that reducing soma-to-injury site distance in htt mutant M-cell axons partially restores regeneration, demonstrating a selective role in long-range CNS axon regeneration. Consistent with a transport-based mechanism, genetic knockdown of htt-associated axonal transport proteins recapitulates the htt mutant regeneration phenotype. Combined, our results provide compelling evidence for a time and distance-sensitive multistep molecular framework in which celsr3 dependent growth rate modulation and htt dependent axonal transport promote spontaneous, long-range spinal cord regeneration.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Pennsylvania, Perelman School of Medicine

title: Brain-wide Cerebrospinal Fluid Recirculation Collapse in Alzheimers Disease
abstract:
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow and the glymphatic system are essential for maintaining brain homeostasis, yet the precise mechanisms driving their profound failure in Alzheimers disease (AD) remain largely elusive. Here, we reveal that macroscopic CSF propagates dorsally via the perivascular spaces (PAS) of major ventral arteries--the Circle of Willis (CW), middle cerebral artery (MCA), and olfactory artery (OlfA)--which undergo severe structural degradation in an AD mouse model. High-resolution imaging of the dorsal cortex demonstrates that this structural collapse induces a severe influx blockade; in AD, CSF tracers form massive aggregates within the PAS, physically decoupling the gliovascular interface, while tracers entering the parenchyma are pathologically sequestered by amyloid plaques. Furthermore, we identify an active, cholesterol-mediated clearance mechanism responding to exogenous CSF tracer infiltration. While healthy brains rapidly synthesize and efficiently clear this cholesterol via vascular efflux within 120 minutes, the AD model exhibits blunted cholesterol mobilization and a complete failure of capillary efflux. This terminal bottleneck forces uncleared cholesterol to retrogradely accumulate into pathological aggregates within perivascular pericytes and neuronal somata. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that AD dismantles the entire CSF recirculation loop--from macroscopic ventral entry to terminal microvascular efflux--highlighting pericytic and neuronal lipidosis as fundamental drivers of brain fluid stagnation.
